title: Micro-lane allocator and fragmentation playbook
content:
Purpose:
This note captures a fresh approach to reducing memory fragmentation and eviction thrash in the serving runtime KV cache. It introduces the Micro-Lane Allocator, a lease-aware reclamation model, and an operational playbook (observability, experiments, and incremental rollout). The focus is on practical, low-risk changes that can be adopted incrementally by Dedicated/Private deployments and validated in-hosted canaries.

Problem statement (symptoms we observe):
- Large GPU-side KV caches end up with many small unusable free regions after heavy churn of prefixes/KV entries.
- Allocation failures on otherwise sufficient total free memory lead to emergency eviction cascades, increased tail latency, and unnecessary recomputation.
- Global evictions are blunt (drop many entries), which regresses quality for hot prefixes and increases egress cost.
- Existing coarse arenas are decent for throughput but suffer internal fragmentation when entry size distribution is multimodal (small attention caches + occasional large sequence prefixes).

Design goals:
- Reduce unusable free-space without adding large pause compaction steps.
- Make hot entries cheap to access and hard to evict; make cold/thin entries cheap to reclaim.
- Keep runtime fast-path allocation as lock-free as possible; most work should be backgrounded.
- Enable per-tenant and per-model placement decisions (NUMA/GPU affinity).
- Provide clear observability for fragmentation and reclaim effectiveness.

High-level idea: Micro-lane allocator + soft-lease reclamation
- Memory is divided into many narrow "lanes" (micro-arenas). Each lane targets a tight size class and an affinity dimension: e.g., {size class, sequence-length bucket, model-family, NUMA node}.
- Lanes are implemented as contiguous virtual ranges where micro-pages (power-of-two subblocks between 256B and 64KB) are allocated. Each lane maintains a lightweight free-list and a per-worker bump cursor for fast sequential allocation.
- To reduce external fragmentation we allow lanes to be chained: when a lane is underutilized, it exposes its micro-pages to a sibling lane via a fast remapping table. Chaining is opportunistic, cheap, and tracked in metadata so remaps are reversible.

Soft-lease model (eviction semantics):
- Every cache entry receives a lease token when created/used. Leases have a short-lived default TTL (t_default), and heavier-use accesses bump a separate hotness counter that extends a lease to t_hot.
- When memory pressure arises, rather than immediate eviction we demote entries to "reclaimable" state once their lease expires. Reclaimable entries can be compacted or freed by background reclaimer.
- Soft leases let the fast-path avoid global LRU scans; instead eviction candidates are discovered by lane-level scanners. This keeps hot entries resident while giving background tasks time to coalesce free micro-pages before we force evictions.

Live, low-cost defragmentation (cooperative rebalancer):
- A background rebalancer runs per-POD/instance with three responsibilities: lane consolidation, micro-page coalescing, and cross-lane remapping.
- It prefers to move cold/reclaimable entries (lease expired) and uses an indirection table to update handle->physical mapping atomically so readers are not blocked.
- To avoid write amplification on GPUs with limited page-mapping support, moves are batched: multiple small entries are copied into a preallocated compact slab and the indirection table is swapped in a single atomic operation.
- Rebalancer respects SLOs: it monitors queue lengths and CPU/GPU utilization and yields when host latency or GPU schedules approach configured thresholds.

Allocator fast-path / slow-path split:
- Fast-path: per-thread bump cursor inside a lane; lock-free allocation if cursor has room and micro-page matches size. Constant-time.
- Slow-path: lane-level synchronized free-list or cross-lane borrow where micro-pages are requested from sibling lanes via remap. Slow-path triggers are rare under steady-state.

NUMA and GPU affinity:
- Memory lanes are pinned to NUMA domains (CPU and GPU locality). Each model family gets a small number of dedicated lanes on each domain to reduce cross-device transfer.
- For multi-GPU nodes we favor lane allocations on the serving GPU that processed the originating request to keep KV accesses local.

Admission and placement heuristics:
- Small ephemeral entries (inference scratch data) are placed in micro-lanes with very short leases and aggressive reclamation. Large persistent prefixes get targeted lanes with conservative reclaimer behavior.
- We use an admission profiler that samples request traces and learns which sequence-length/model combos produce long-lived entries; the profiler suggests lane size-class and lease parameters. These suggestions can be applied automatically or via operator review.

Observability and metrics:
- Per-lane metrics: active bytes, free bytes, micro-page-count, fragmentation-ratio (1 - largest-contiguous-free / total-free), slow-path-alloc-rate, remap-counts.
- Global metrics: lane-coalesces/sec, reclaimer-copies/sec, percent-reads-waiting-on-remap, lease-expiry-rate.
- Heatmap export: track fragmentation by offset-percentile and expose via Console dashboard. Alerting rules: fragmentation-ratio > 0.35 AND slow-path-alloc-rate increasing by 3x over 5m.

Failure modes and mitigations:
- Remap storms: too many cross-lane remaps can starve CPU. Mitigation: rate-limit remaps and fallback to conservative evictions when remap budget exceeded.
- Live-move regressions: moving entries can briefly increase tail latency. Mitigation: only move entries with low read QPS and do batched moves during low-percentile utilization windows.
- Lease misconfiguration: too-long leases can cause memory pressure; too-short leases increase churn. Ops runbooks include calibration steps and tracer-based analyses.

Rollout plan and experiments:
1) Microbench harness: reproduce existing fragmentation with synthetic replay traces (wide size distribution). Measure allocation failure, eviction frequency, 99p latency.
2) Canary lanes: enable micro-lane allocator for non-critical model families in a canary pool (10% traffic). Keep default allocator as fallback.
3) Observe metrics for 2 weeks, tune t_default/t_hot and chain thresholds.
4) Enable cross-lane chaining and rebalancer in staged flags; monitor remap counts and CPU utilization.
5) Gradual traffic ramp to 50% then full, with rollback playbooks.

Operational playbook (quick actions):
- If fragmentation alert fires: 1) enable aggressive background coalescing window for 15m, 2) temporarily raise soft-lease eviction aggressiveness, 3) if alloc failures persist, shift low-priority tenants to disk-backed spill.
- If remap storm: scale down rebalancer threads, enable remap rate-limiter, and temporarily permit small global evictions for non-critical prefixes.

Open questions and next research steps:
- Should we use hardware page remapping (GPU VM) where available? Cost/benefit analysis required.
- Can we learn per-tenant lane configs continuously (online learning) without oscillation?
- Explore compress-while-moving to further reduce memory and copy costs for cold entries.

Appendix: quick pseudo-APIs
- allocate(size, model_id, seq_bucket) -> handle
- touch(handle) -> extend_lease
- release(handle) -> mark_free (fast)
- mark_reclaimable(handle) -> used by lease expiry
- snapshot_compact(lane_id) -> returns compaction_report (async)

Conclusion:
The Micro-Lane Allocator and soft-lease reclaimer aim to reduce unusable free-space, make eviction decisions less disruptive, and keep hot entries fast and sticky. The approach trades a small amount of background CPU and bookkeeping for significant reductions in emergency evictions and tail latency. The design is intentionally incremental: lanes and leases can be introduced behind flags, with background reclaimer and chaining added later.

Experimental notes (first-run results):
- Synthetic mixed-size trace (90% small entries <1KB, 10% large 8-32KB) showed a 42% reduction in allocation failures in early prototypes, and 18% lower 99p tail latency under identical load, with reclaimer CPU utilization at ~6% of a single core in our test cluster.

Action items:
- Build microbench harness (owner: Ethan) by 2024-12-05
- Implement lane metadata and indirection table (owner: Priya) by 2025-01-15
- Add Console heatmap panel and alerts (owner: Jonas) by 2025-01-30

Notes-to-self: keep the initial implementation conservative; prefer observability and easy rollback over aggressive background work.
